> **The research decision.** Decide which single attribute you will vary between
> otherwise identical cases, what response you will count, and whose time and consent
> your design uses to get it. No tool can make those choices for you, because each one
> fixes what your number describes and who pays for it.

## Why this decision matters

**The decision on the table: which one thing differs between your cases, and what
your difference in responses is allowed to say.**

> *"You sent the same résumé under two names and one name got more calls. Fine. Now
> tell me what the name told the employer. Was it race, or class, or a region, or all
> three? Tell me which employers you wrote to, and when. And tell me why you counted
> each email as a case when forty of them landed on the same desk."*
> — a **labor economist**, refereeing a correspondence study of hiring

An audit study looks simple, and that is its trap. You build two cases that differ in
one attribute, send them out, and count replies. The count arrives quickly and looks
decisive. But the attribute you varied may carry several signals at once. The replies
may come from a handful of decision makers counted many times over. And the people
who answered never agreed to take part. Get these wrong and a clean-looking gap
describes something other than what your headline says, with more confidence than your
data hold. This chapter gives you the decisions that make an audit's number mean what
you claim, whether the decision maker is a person or an AI system.

## The concept

This chapter follows the audit-experiment design in the experimental-descriptive
section of the RDSS design library [@blair2023rdss]. RDSS files the audit there on
purpose. The coin flip decides which version of a case a decision maker sees, but the
question RDSS asks is descriptive: how many decision makers in the sample treat the two
versions differently. Randomization works here as a measuring instrument. RDSS also
grants that the same randomized contrast can be read causally, as the average effect of
sending one version instead of the other, and that this reading is correct. So place
your question on the inquiry compass, not your instrument. "How many of these employers
treat the two names differently?" is descriptive. "Does a name that signals this group
change the callback rate?" is causal, and the random assignment of the version is what
licenses that answer for the cases you sent. Either way, the reach is set by how you
chose the decision makers. Drawn from a defined list, your answer can reach that list.
Taken as whoever was convenient, it stays with the ones you wrote to, and you say so.

An **audit study** is a design that sends matched cases, identical except for one
attribute you choose, to real decision makers and records how each case is treated.
Example: two testers with the same scripted qualifications apply in person for the
same jobs, and only one of them reports a criminal record [@pager2003mark].

A **correspondence study** is an audit carried out entirely on paper or online, with
fictitious applications instead of trained testers. Example: fictitious résumés sent
in response to help-wanted ads in Boston and Chicago newspapers, with names chosen to
sound White or Black, where the White-sounding names received about 50 percent more callbacks
[@bertrand2004emily]. Correspondence studies are cheaper and remove the tester's
behaviour from the comparison, which is one reason they are now common.

You can deliver the two versions in two ways. **Matched pairs** means each decision
maker receives both versions, in randomized order. Example: every employer gets one
application from each name set, a few days apart. **Randomized single cases** means
each decision maker receives only one version, chosen by a coin flip. Example: each
legislator gets one email asking for help, signed with a name chosen to sound Black
or White [@butler2011politicians]. Pairs give more precision per decision maker. Single cases
are harder for a decision maker to notice, because nobody sees two near-identical
letters arrive in the same week.

Now the hard part. The **signal problem** is the fact that the attribute you vary
usually carries more than one message. Example: a name can signal race and also social
class, and names given mostly by more educated Black mothers are less often perceived
as Black than names given by less educated mothers [@gaddis2017black]. Your gap
therefore measures the response to *this name as read by these decision makers*. Before
you write "race," you owe the reader evidence that the names signal race and little
else. Pretesting how people perceive the names is the standard way to get it.

The **estimand**, the exact quantity your design is built to state, is narrow. It is
the **net response gap**: the difference in response rates between the two versions,
for these decision makers, these postings, and this period. Random assignment of the
version is the warrant for it, and it needs nothing more. RDSS's descriptive target is
a different number: the share of decision makers who would respond to the first version
but not to the second. The net gap equals that share only if almost nobody discriminates
in the reverse direction. If some do, the net gap subtracts them from the others. It then
understates the share who favour the first version, and it can sit near zero while
many decision makers discriminate, in both directions [@blair2023rdss]. So report the
net gap as what you measured. Write the word "share" only with that assumption stated
beside it and defended for your decision makers. The warrant for extending the gap
beyond the decision makers you reached is sampling. If you drew them from a defined list, such as every posting on a
job board during one month, you may speak about that list. If you took whoever was
convenient, you describe the ones you reached.

What the design cannot establish matters as much. An audit does not tell you *why*
decision makers responded differently. Dislike of a group and a crude guess about
productivity produce the same callback gap. It does not tell you what happens to wages
or hires further down the line. It does not say how often real applicants face the gap
either, because real applicants do not send identical résumés.

Two further terms protect the analysis. **Clustering** means that several responses
come from the same decision maker or the same posting, so they rise and fall together
instead of counting as separate cases. Example: forty applications sent to one national retailer may all
be screened by the same recruiter under the same rule. Count the decision maker as the
case, or compute an interval that allows for the grouping. Otherwise your interval
will be too narrow. The **post-treatment trap** is comparing the *quality* of replies,
such as tone or warmth, only among the decision makers who replied. Example: someone
who never answers one name leaves no email whose tone you could score. So a tone
comparison among repliers compares different kinds of people [@coppock2019avoiding].
Keep the response rate as your main outcome, and treat any quality measure as a
separate analysis with its own assumptions.

## Whose time, and whose consent

Audits of people carry an ethical cost that most designs do not. The decision makers
did not agree to take part. The design only works if they do not know. You spend their
time reading applications that do not exist. Any fictitious applicant who gets an
invitation may hold an interview slot a real applicant needed, and a pair design
doubles the letters each decision maker reads. That is why human audits need a formal
determination before you send a single case. The
[ethics chapter](../part2-curiosity-to-design/research-ethics-and-data-governance.qmd)
walks you through the permission status. Expect a review board to ask you to justify
waiving consent, to withdraw each fictitious application quickly once someone replies,
and to say whether and how you will debrief the people you wrote to.

For a project that has one term to run, the realistic human route is reanalysis. Some
published audits have released their data, and a careful replication or a new question
asked of an existing audit dataset is a real contribution that needs no deception at
all. If you still want to collect, the route in the rest of this chapter sits entirely
outside human subjects: auditing an AI system.

## Auditing an AI system

The same logic now tests machines. An **algorithm audit** is an audit study whose
decision maker is an automated system, observed from the outside by feeding it
controlled inputs and recording what it returns [@metaxa2021auditing]. Example:
researchers created fake accounts that differed only in browser, operating system,
or shopping history, ran the same searches on e-commerce sites, and recorded where
prices and product rankings differed. They also had to separate those differences
from ordinary noise such as inventory changes [@hannak2014measuring].
Another example comes from facial analysis. Commercial gender classifiers misclassified
darker-skinned women far more often than lighter-skinned men [@buolamwini2018gender].
Researchers have also varied the names inside prompts to a language model and found
that its advice shifted with the name [@salinas2024name]. That study is a preprint,
so read it as a design example, not a settled result. In biology, you could audit a
plant-identification app by photographing the same specimens under randomized lighting
and backgrounds and recording which conditions make it fail.

An AI audit of a tool you query yourself deceives no person, but it still has rules
and traps. Read the tool's terms of use before you send a single call, and never feed
test cases into a live system where they land in a real person's queue, such as an
employer's actual applicant pipeline. An AI partner is genuinely useful for the
mechanical half: generating many template variants, running calls on a schedule, and
logging every output with its build string. The traps below are where it needs you.

- **Frozen configuration** is the practice of recording the model's exact version,
  the date, and every setting before the first call, and keeping them fixed for the
  whole run. Example: the vendor's build string copied from the settings page, the
  temperature, and the system instructions, saved in your run record. A model can be
  updated overnight without notice. An audit that spans an update has measured two
  systems and blended them. That silent change is called **drift**.
- **Temperature** is the setting that controls how much a model's output varies when
  you send the identical input again. Example: at a low temperature the same résumé
  gets nearly the same score every time; at a high one the score wanders.
- **Nested outputs** means that repeated outputs for the same prompt all come from one
  case. They still answer a question, only a narrow one. Example: fifty runs of one
  résumé under each name, on one frozen build, estimate how that build treats *that
  résumé*. For that estimand each run is a fair draw, and the run is the unit. They
  tell you almost nothing about the other résumés the model will meet. For a claim
  about how the screener treats résumés, the case is the template, exactly as the
  decision maker is the case in a human audit. Write down which of the two questions
  you are asking before you choose the unit. At a temperature of zero, repeats may
  return nearly the same output and add little even to the narrow question.
- A **scoring rule** is the written definition of what counts as a favourable
  response, fixed by you before you see any output. Example: "advance means a score
  of 7 or more out of 10," or "the reply recommends an interview." If you let another
  model judge the outputs, that **evaluator model** is a second instrument with its
  own errors. It is not ground truth. Check it against your own reading of a random
  subset before you trust its labels.

## A worked example

Bring this into a business setting. A small firm is deciding whether to adopt an AI
résumé screener. Before it does, you audit the screener. You write 60 résumé
templates spanning the firm's usual applicants. Each template is sent twice, once under
a name drawn at random from set A and once under a name from set B. The two sets were
pretested so that readers perceive them as differing in one group signal and not in
class. Order is randomized, so neither name set always goes first, and any slow change in the
tool over the afternoon cannot line up with one name set. The run record is
written before the first call: build string, date, temperature, and the scoring rule.
Everything is run in one afternoon.

This is the matched-pair logic of the classic correspondence study, moved from
employers to software [@bertrand2004emily]. The template is the case. The estimand is
the difference in advance rates between the name sets, for this screener build, these
name sets, these 60 templates, and these settings.

The block below uses a constructed screener in which a set-B name costs half a point on
average. Watch the table of pairs: only the templates where the two names split carry
information about the gap.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# Written BEFORE the first call, and never edited afterward.
run_record = {"tool": "resume screener, build string copied from its settings page",
              "date": "one afternoon, all calls", "temperature": 0,
              "rule": "advance = score of 7 or more out of 10"}

n = 60                                           # résumé templates = the cases
quality = rng.uniform(4, 9, n)                   # how strong each résumé reads
sent_first = np.where(rng.random(n) < 0.5, "set A", "set B")  # order, randomized
# CONSTRUCTED screener: a name from set B costs half a point on average.
score_a = np.clip(np.round(quality + rng.normal(0, 1.0, n)), 0, 10)
score_b = np.clip(np.round(quality - 0.5 + rng.normal(0, 1.0, n)), 0, 10)
adv_a, adv_b = score_a >= 7, score_b >= 7        # the rule, fixed in advance

pairs = pd.crosstab(pd.Series(adv_a, name="set A advanced"),
                    pd.Series(adv_b, name="set B advanced"))
print(f"set A name sent first : {np.mean(sent_first == 'set A')*100:.0f}% of templates")
print(pairs, "\n")
d = adv_a.astype(float) - adv_b                  # one difference per template
gap, se = d.mean(), d.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)
print(f"advance rate, set A names : {adv_a.mean()*100:.0f}%")
print(f"advance rate, set B names : {adv_b.mean()*100:.0f}%")
print(f"name gap                  : {gap*100:+.1f} points")
print(f"95% interval (templates)  : {(gap-1.96*se)*100:+.1f} to {(gap+1.96*se)*100:+.1f}")
print("\nonly the templates where the two names split carry the gap;")
print("this describes THIS tool, THIS build, THESE résumés")
```

Read the output as a referee would. Set-A names advanced on 62 percent of templates
and set-B names on 48 percent. Most templates did not split at all: both names
advanced on 28 and neither on 22. The gap comes from 10 templates, 9 where only the
set-A name advanced and 1 where only the set-B name did. That net 8 templates out of
60 is the gap of 13.3 points, with a 95 percent interval from 3.5 to 23.2. Do not read
the 9 as a count of templates the screener treats unfairly. In this constructed
screener every template pays the same half point on average, and ordinary score noise
alone makes pairs split in both directions. The net difference is the gap; the split
counts are not a head count of penalised cases. The
interval is wide because 60 templates are not many, and each template counts once.
It also treats your 60 templates as a draw from the kinds of résumés the firm
receives. You earn that reading by how you built them. Templates adapted from a
random sample of the firm's past applications, with personal details removed, earn
it better than 60 résumés you invented at your desk.

The sentence you may write: "On 60 templates, this screener build advanced set-A
names on about 13 more templates in every 100 than set-B names (95 percent interval
roughly 4 to 23), under the settings in our run record." The sentences you may not
write are about every build of the tool, about the firm's real applicant pool, or
about the screener's intent. The constructed half-point penalty is also an idea of the
example. In a real audit you do not know the truth, which is the reason for the
interval.

## A seeded simulation

Two claims from this chapter can be checked by simulation. The first: an audit's
interval shrinks only as the number of *cases* grows. The second: repeating the same
prompt many times does not add cases for a question about résumés in general, and
treating those repeats as cases produces an interval that looks precise and misses
that target. The code below builds a screener whose true name gap is 6 points on average across résumés. Some résumés trigger a
large gap, some almost none, and about four in ten lean toward the other name. So the
6 points is a net gap. Reading it as the share of résumés the screener penalises would
be wrong here, because the reverse cases pull it down. The seed makes the
run reproduce exactly.

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
TRUE_GAP = 0.06                                   # 6 points, by construction

def templates(n):
    base = rng.uniform(0.40, 0.60, n)             # advance rate with a set-A name
    gap = rng.uniform(-0.24, 0.36, n)             # the name gap differs by résumé
    return base, base - gap                       # rates for set A, set B

# Left: one run per name per template, audits of growing size.
sizes, est, half = [10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320], [], []
for n in sizes:
    pa, pb = templates(n)
    d = (rng.random(n) < pa).astype(float) - (rng.random(n) < pb)
    est.append(100 * d.mean())
    half.append(100 * 1.96 * d.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n))
    print(f"{n:>3} templates: gap {est[-1]:+6.1f}, 95% interval "
          f"{est[-1]-half[-1]:+6.1f} to {est[-1]+half[-1]:+6.1f}")

# Right: 10 templates x 50 repeated runs per name = 1,000 outputs, rerun 1,000 times.
J, K, T_9 = 10, 50, 2.262                         # T_9: t value for 9 df
hits_naive = hits_clust = 0
for r in range(1000):
    pa, pb = templates(J)
    ya = rng.random((J, K)) < pa[:, None]
    yb = rng.random((J, K)) < pb[:, None]
    gap = ya.mean() - yb.mean()
    se_naive = np.sqrt((ya.mean()*(1-ya.mean()) + yb.mean()*(1-yb.mean())) / (J*K))
    se_clust = (ya.mean(axis=1) - yb.mean(axis=1)).std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(J)
    hits_naive += abs(gap - TRUE_GAP) <= 1.96 * se_naive
    hits_clust += abs(gap - TRUE_GAP) <= T_9 * se_clust
    if r == 0:                                    # keep the first audit to plot
        g0 = 100 * gap
        ci = {"naive": (g0 - 196*se_naive, g0 + 196*se_naive),
              "clustered": (g0 - 100*T_9*se_clust, g0 + 100*T_9*se_clust)}
print(f"\nfirst audit, gap {g0:+.1f}")
for k, (lo, hi) in ci.items():
    print(f"  {k:9s} interval : {lo:+.1f} to {hi:+.1f}")
print(f"\nnaive intervals cover the truth     : {hits_naive/10:.0f}% of reruns")
print(f"clustered intervals cover the truth : {hits_clust/10:.0f}% of reruns")

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.6))
a1.errorbar(range(6), est, yerr=half, fmt="o", color="#2a78d6", capsize=3)
a1.axhline(100 * TRUE_GAP, color="#333333", ls="--")
a1.set_xticks(range(6), sizes)
a1.set_xlabel("Résumé templates in the audit (one run per name)")
a1.set_ylabel("Name gap in advance rate (points)")
for y, (k, col) in enumerate([("clustered", "#2a78d6"), ("naive", "#eb6834")]):
    a2.plot(ci[k], [y, y], color=col, lw=3)
    a2.plot([g0], [y], "o", color=col)
a2.axvline(100 * TRUE_GAP, color="#333333", ls="--")
a2.axvline(0, color="#999999", lw=.8)
a2.set_yticks([0, 1], ["clustered", "naive"])
a2.set_xlabel("Name gap in advance rate (points)")
plt.show()
```

![More résumé templates narrow the interval around the 6-point gap, while 1,000
repeated outputs from 10 templates produce a naive interval that is far too
narrow.](../images/sims/audit_studies.png){fig-alt="Two-panel chart. Left: blue dots
with vertical 95 percent interval bars for audits of 10, 20, 40, 80, 160 and 320 résumé
templates, with a dashed line at the true gap of 6 points; the interval runs from
minus 55.7 to plus 35.7 at 10 templates and narrows to plus 0.2 to plus 15.5 at 320.
Right: two horizontal intervals for the same audit of 1,000 outputs, estimate 8.6
points; the orange naive interval runs from 2.5 to 14.7 and covers the truth in 67
percent of 1,000 reruns; the blue clustered interval runs from minus 6.4 to 23.6 and
covers the truth in 94 percent of reruns; a dashed line marks the true gap of 6 and a
grey line marks zero."}

Read the left panel first. With 10 templates, the estimate came out at minus 10.0
points, pointing the wrong way, with an interval from minus 55.7 to plus 35.7. That
interval is honest: 10 cases cannot tell a large gap from none. With 320 templates the
estimate is 7.8 and the interval runs from plus 0.2 to plus 15.5, close to the true 6
and narrow enough to say something. The estimates wander on the way, and at 20
templates one run landed at plus 30.0. Each audit is a single draw, which is why the
interval travels with the estimate every time.

Now the right panel. The same 1,000 outputs, 10 templates run 50 times per name, give
one estimate of 8.6 points and two intervals. The naive interval treats every output
as a new case and runs from 2.5 to 14.7. It excludes zero and looks like a finding.
The clustered interval treats each template as one case and runs from minus 6.4 to
23.6, which is what 10 cases can actually support. The true gap here is the average
over all the résumés the screener might meet, so the number of templates, not the
number of outputs, sets the precision. Across 1,000 reruns of the whole audit, the
naive interval covered the true gap only 67 percent of the time, against a promised 95.
The clustered interval covered it 94 percent of the time. The naive interval is not
wrong about everything. For a narrower target, the average gap on these 10 templates
alone, its width is about right. It fails because the question was about résumés the
audit never sent. Repeating a prompt measures how that prompt fares. It does not tell
you how the model treats résumés you did not send. In the companion notebook, change `J, K, T_9` to
`40, 12, 2.023` (2.023 is the t value for 39 degrees of freedom). The audit then
spends about the same budget on more templates. Watch the two intervals move closer
together and the naive coverage climb toward the clustered one.

## An AI failure case

You ask an agentic tool to run your screener audit. You give it one résumé template
and two name sets, and it comes back with a tidy report. "I ran the prompt 50 times
for each name (n = 50 per group). Set-A names advanced in 41 of 50 runs, set-B names
in 29 of 50, a statistically significant difference of 24 points." The code ran, the
numbers add up, and the table is clean.

This is two named failures. It is **plausible-but-wrong-method**, because the report
treats 100 draws from one case as if they were 100 independent résumés. The test
itself answers a real but narrow question: on one frozen build, does this one template
advance more often under one name set? For that estimand, 50 runs per name are fair
draws. It is also **silent scope change**, because a statement about one résumé became
a finding about the screener. The arithmetic is fine; the unit is wrong for the claim.
For any claim about the screener's treatment of résumés, the audit has one case, and
the right sample size is 1. Read its log closely and a third problem appears, and it
breaks even the narrow reading. Halfway through the run, the tool's calls started
returning a different build string. The vendor had pushed an update, so the 50 runs
per name straddle two systems and are not draws from one set of outputs.

A tidy count is not a sample. You catch it by asking the question the report skipped:
*what is the case here, and how many of them are there?* Then you check the build
string on every output line against your run record. Rewrite the result as what it
is: "For one template, under builds X and Y, set-A names advanced more often," and
split the runs by build before you test even that. Then
rerun the audit with many templates on one frozen build, and log why.

*Your design is declared and diagnosed. This route asks you to name the one attribute
you will vary, the case your number is about, and whose time the design spends.*

The hands-on half of this section lives in the chapter's **companion notebook**: open it in Colab with the badge at the top, and work the steps there.

Commit your own answer first, then delegate. Each prompt below is a checkable job, not
a request for a verdict. Work them as a loop. The first answer is a draft: find the
claim you cannot check, say so in your next message, and run it again. Some tools will
run a whole audit unattended and hand you a finished report. That is exactly when you
check what the case was and which build answered.

::: {.callout-important title="Do not delegate"}
Three calls stay yours. You decide **which attribute you vary and what it signals**,
because the meaning of a name or a photo is a judgment about how decision makers read
it. You decide **what counts as a favourable response**, and you write that scoring
rule before you see a single output. And you decide **whether this audit may be run at
all**: whose time it spends, whether it deceives anyone, and what permission it needs.
A tool can draft cases, run calls, and tabulate replies. You own the claim, its unit,
and its boundary.
:::

1. Write your audit question as one sentence naming the decision maker, the attribute,
   and the response. Underneath it, write the estimand: the net difference in response
   rates, for which decision makers or which system build, over which cases and which
   period. Say whether the question is descriptive (how many treat the versions
   differently) or causal (what sending one version instead of the other does).
2. Name the attribute's signals. List everything your chosen names, photos, or phrases
   might tell a reader besides the one attribute you intend. Then say how you will
   check what they actually signal.

   Commit your own list before you delegate.

   *When you are ready to delegate this step:*

   ```text
   I plan an audit that varies [attribute] using these versions: [paste your
   names, photos, or phrases]. Act as a skeptical sociologist. List every
   attribute a reader might infer from each version besides the one I intend,
   in a table with the version, the extra signal, and which direction it could
   push my response gap. Do not suggest replacement versions; I will choose them.
   ```

   After running, verify: compare the table with the list you wrote first, and look
   for a published pretest of how people perceive your versions before you trust
   either list. Counters **illusion of completeness** (a tidy table that omits the
   one signal your reader will raise first).
3. Declare your case and your data strategy. Say what one case is (a decision maker, a
   posting, a template), how many you will have, how they were chosen, and whether
   each case gets both versions or one. If you plan repeated runs of one prompt, say
   whether they serve a claim about that prompt or only steady its score. If you are auditing an AI system, write the
   run record now: build string, date, every setting, and the scoring rule.
4. Declare your answer strategy and its warrant. State the comparison you will compute,
   which is the net gap, and the interval you will attach to it with the case as the
   unit. If you also want to call the gap a share of decision makers who discriminate,
   state the assumption that reading needs (almost no one favours the other version)
   and why it is plausible for your decision makers; if you cannot defend it, report
   the net gap alone. Then say
   which population, if any, your sampling lets you speak about, and write one
   sentence on what the audit cannot establish: why the decision makers responded as
   they did, or what real applicants face.

   *When you are ready to delegate this step:*

   ```text
   Here is my audit plan: [paste steps 1 to 4]. Act as a hostile referee of
   audit studies. Tell me where my responses are not independent cases for the
   claim I state: the same decision maker, the same posting, the same prompt,
   or the same model build. For each, say what the true number of cases is.
   Do not rewrite the plan for me.
   ```

   After running, verify: count your cases by hand from your own plan and compare the
   number with the referee's. If it only praises the plan, push back with "assume my
   interval is too narrow; name the reason." Counters **sycophantic agreement**
   (praise that reviews your ego, not your evidence).
5. Settle the permission question. If real people receive your cases, write your
   permission status and the competent authority you will ask. Then write the
   no-deception route you will take if the answer is no: reanalysis of a published
   audit's open data, or an audit of an AI system.

   *When you are ready to delegate this step:*

   ```text
   Act as a research librarian in economics and political science. Find
   published correspondence or audit studies whose authors released their
   response-level data. For each give authors, year, venue, the attribute
   varied, and where the data are archived. Only include work you are
   confident exists; mark anything uncertain.
   ```

   After running, verify: open each archive yourself and download the file before you
   cite it; treat any study or dataset you cannot find as a possible **confident
   fabrication** and leave it out.
6. Log the step in your AI Research Ledger, and verify at least one output with a named
   method from the [Verification Guide](../verification-guide.qmd). A **benchmark
   result** is the natural check for an audit's pipeline: run it on a published
   audit's open data, or on the worked example above, and confirm it reproduces the
   reported gap and interval within rounding. A **falsification test** is the strong
   second check. Send a slice of cases where both versions carry the same name. If
   your setup is sound, that gap should sit near zero within its interval; a clear gap
   there means something besides the name differs, such as order or a changed build.
   A gap near zero is reassuring; it does not show the pipeline is flawless. An AI reviewer
   may run the checks with you; the decision to accept or reject stays yours.
